title: Why Is Subnautica Scary Before Anything Attacks?

research.citation: Grillon, Baas, Lissek, Smith & Milstein (2004), Anxious responses to predictable and unpredictable aversive events, Behavioral Neuroscience 118(5):916–924
research.claim: Experiment comparing predictable vs unpredictable aversive events: unpredictable shock contexts heightened sustained startle; this effect was absent for less aversive airblast condition. Does not directly study game players.

research.citation: Mobbs et al. (2007), When Fear Is Near: Threat Imminence Elicits Prefrontal-Periaqueductal Gray Shifts in Humans, Science 317:1079–1083
research.claim: In a virtual predator chase experiment, neural response patterns shifted as the predator approached; greater dread correlated with imminence. Not a Subnautica-specific experiment.

description: A research-informed mini lesson exploring predictable vs uncertain threat, startle reactions and threat imminence, illustrated with real Subnautica gameplay. Clarifies that psychology lab research does not directly prove how all Subnautica players react. 110 seconds; soundtrack and text captions only. Production review v2: replace base-tour recording with actual underwater leviathan confrontations. Final footage-only review revision: Leviathan pursuit gameplay, avoiding branded interstitials.
youtube_title: Why Is Subnautica Terrifying BEFORE Anything Attacks? | Gaming Psychology
social_caption:
Why can the ocean in Subnautica feel terrifying even when there's nothing in sight? 🌊 Psychology gives us two clues: unpredictable threats can sustain anxious anticipation, and our response changes as danger draws closer. We explore the science using real Subnautica gameplay — without claiming that laboratory findings are direct proof about every player.

Research: Grillon et al. (2004), DOI: 10.1037/0735-7044.118.5.916; Mobbs et al. (2007), DOI: 10.1126/science.1144298.

What's scarier: the empty water or seeing the Reaper? 🎮🧠
